lessonTitle: Specimen Handling and Staining: From Fixation to H&E

blocks.text: A small prostate needle biopsy arrives in a pot labelled with only a surname. Two other men with the same surname were biopsied that morning. A cancer diagnosis assigned to the wrong man could lead to a needless radical operation for one and a missed cancer for another. The journey from patient to glass slide depends as much on discipline as on science.

blocks.markdown: A diagnosis is only as reliable as the slide it is made from. Tissue removed from the body begins to degrade immediately, so it must be identified, preserved (fixed), processed into a form that can be cut very thinly, and stained so that structures become visible. This unit follows a specimen from fixation to haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and explains why labelling and fixation errors cannot be corrected later.

blocks.title: Fixation
blocks.text: Fixation preserves tissue by stopping autolysis (self-digestion by the cell's own enzymes) and bacterial decay and by stabilising proteins. The standard fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin, which forms cross-links between proteins. A usual rule is a volume of fixative at least 10 times the volume of the specimen, and tissue should be placed in fixative promptly because delay (cold ischaemia) degrades proteins and nucleic acids that tests later rely on.

items: Dehydration through graded alcohols to remove water
Clearing in a solvent such as xylene, miscible with both alcohol and wax
Microtomy: cutting sections about 3 to 5 micrometres thick and floating them onto glass slides
Deparaffinising and staining (H&E), then dehydrating and mounting under a coverslip

rows: Prevent autolysis and decay, cross-link proteins
Remove water so wax can enter
Replace alcohol with a wax-miscible solvent
Support tissue so it can be cut thin
blocks.caption: Steps in routine histology processing.

Minimum fixation time t for fixative to reach the centre of a tissue slice; d is the distance the fixative must travel from each exposed face (mm) and v is the penetration rate, about 1 mm per hour for formalin (an approximate teaching value).

blocks.title: How long to fix a tissue slice
blocks.prompt: A slice of liver 10 mm thick is placed flat in formalin so fixative can enter from both faces. Using a penetration rate of 1 mm per hour, estimate the minimum time for fixative to reach the centre.

steps.text: Fixative enters from the top and bottom, so each face only has to reach the middle of the slice, a distance of half the thickness.
Calculate the distance from each face.

blocks.answer: At least 5 hours; routine fixation is usually longer (commonly 6 to 48 hours) to allow cross-linking to be completed.

blocks.markdown: **H&E staining.** Haematoxylin, oxidised to haematein and used with an aluminium mordant, behaves as a basic dye, so it binds acidic structures: nuclei (DNA) appear blue-purple. Eosin is an acidic dye that binds basic proteins, colouring cytoplasm, collagen and muscle in shades of pink. Slides are dehydrated with alcohol and cleared before mounting.

**Why labelling and fixation matter.** Two patient identifiers, the specimen site, laterality, date and time of collection and relevant clinical details must be on the container and the request form and must match. A wrongly labelled or unlabelled specimen risks a wrong-patient diagnosis, which is a serious patient-safety event and may result in the specimen being rejected. Poor fixation (too little formalin, delay before fixation, or fixation that is too short or too long) produces poor morphology and can falsely alter immunohistochemistry such as oestrogen receptor and HER2, which can change treatment decisions. Neither error can be fixed after processing.

rows: Small piece of tissue (core, punch, endoscopic forceps)
Sampling error; does not show whole lesion
Surgical removal of a tumour or organ
Large; needs orientation and careful sampling
Cells in a smear, fluid or fine needle aspirate
Tissue architecture not seen; invasion hard to prove

blocks.title: Estimating fixative volume
blocks.prompt: A surgeon places a 36 mL polyp in a container. Using the rule of at least 10 times the specimen volume, calculate the minimum volume of formalin.

steps.text: The rule is fixative volume at least 10 times the specimen volume.
If the container holds less than this, a larger one is needed to avoid under-fixation.

blocks.answer: At least 360 mL of 10% neutral buffered formalin.

blocks.title: Mislabelled or unfixed specimens
blocks.text: Do not guess identity or fixative history. Return the specimen and request form to the sender for clarification, record the delay if fixation was late, and report the incident, because errors made before the lab receives the specimen cannot be corrected by the laboratory.

points: Routine processing runs from fixation through dehydration, clearing and wax embedding to cutting and H&E staining, where haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple and eosin stains cytoplasm pink.
Accurate labelling and prompt adequate fixation protect patient identity and the quality of morphology and immunohistochemistry.
Biopsy samples tissue for diagnosis, resection removes a lesion or organ for staging and margins, and cytology examines cells without tissue architecture.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of fixing a tissue specimen in formalin?

options.text: To stop autolysis and decay and stabilise proteins
To make the tissue transparent for staining

questions.correctOptionText: To stop autolysis and decay and stabilise proteins

distractorRationale.b: Fat is dissolved by clearing solvents, and is not the purpose of fixation.

questions.explanation: Fixation preserves tissue by cross-linking proteins and inactivating degradative enzymes. Without it, tissue autolyses and the structure that the pathologist needs is lost.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the main steps from specimen to stained slide?

options.text: Fixation, dehydration, clearing, wax infiltration, embedding, cutting, staining

questions.correctOptionText: Fixation, dehydration, clearing, wax infiltration, embedding, cutting, staining

distractorRationale.d: Embedding follows infiltration, and staining occurs after cutting.

questions.explanation: Water must be removed by alcohols and replaced with a wax-miscible solvent before wax can penetrate. Sections are cut from the embedded block, then stained.

questions.stem: In an H&E stained section, which structures are stained blue-purple?

distractorRationale.d: Red cells are bright pink to red with eosin.

questions.explanation: Haematoxylin is a basic dye that binds acidic nucleic acids in the nucleus. Eosin, an acidic dye, stains proteins such as cytoplasm and collagen pink.

questions.stem: A breast core biopsy is left on a bench for 3 hours before being placed in formalin. What is the most important concern?

options.text: Antigen degradation that may give false oestrogen receptor or HER2 results
Wax will not infiltrate the tissue
The specimen will become a cytology sample

questions.correctOptionText: Antigen degradation that may give false oestrogen receptor or HER2 results

distractorRationale.a: Correct: delayed fixation damages proteins and nucleic acids.
distractorRationale.b: Wax infiltration is unaffected by this delay in principle.

questions.explanation: Cold ischaemia time damages labile proteins and phosphoproteins, so IHC results may be unreliable. Because ER and HER2 guide treatment, this is clinically important.

questions.stem: A surgeon removes a segment of colon containing a tumour to determine the pT stage and margin status. Which specimen type is this?

distractorRationale.b: A biopsy samples a small piece for diagnosis.
distractorRationale.d: A smear is a cytology specimen.

questions.explanation: A resection removes the lesion or organ so that the whole tumour can be staged and margins assessed. Biopsies and cytology cannot provide this information.

questions.stem: A cytology specimen preserves the full tissue architecture and can reliably demonstrate invasion.
questions.explanation: Cytology examines individual cells or small clusters and does not show tissue architecture. Invasion is demonstrated in histological sections of tissue.

questions.stem: A kidney slice 14 mm thick is fixed flat so formalin enters from both faces. Assuming a penetration rate of 1 mm/h, calculate the minimum time in hours for fixative to reach the centre.
questions.explanation: The distance from each face to the centre is 14 / 2 = 7 mm, so the time is 7 mm divided by 1 mm/h, which is 7 h. Routine protocols use longer fixation to complete cross-linking.

questions.stem: A paraffin block contains a tissue core 1.6 mm deep. A microtome cuts 4 micrometre sections. Ignoring trimming and wastage, what is the maximum number of sections?
questions.explanation: Convert 1.6 mm to 1600 micrometres and divide by 4 micrometres to give 400 sections. In practice fewer are obtained after trimming, so levels should be planned if many stains are needed.

questions.stem: A pathology laboratory receives an unlabelled container and a request form for a 63-year-old man with a lung mass. Explain why correct specimen labelling and fixation matter, giving two consequences of error and what should be done.
markingGuide: Two patient identifiers, site and date must match container and form
Mislabelling risks wrong-patient diagnosis and wrong treatment
Unlabelled specimen should not be processed until identity is confirmed or it should be rejected per policy
Prompt fixation in adequate volume of formalin prevents autolysis
Delayed or poor fixation damages morphology and immunohistochemistry
Errors cannot be corrected after processing
questions.explanation: Pre-analytical errors are the commonest source of serious laboratory incidents. Marking should reward both patient safety and diagnostic quality arguments.

questions.stem: Differentiate biopsy, resection and cytology specimens. For each, give one example, what it can answer and one limitation.
markingGuide: Biopsy: small tissue sample, for example core or endoscopic, to make a diagnosis
Biopsy limitation: sampling error or incomplete representation
Resection: removal of lesion or organ, gives stage, grade and margins
Resection limitation: requires careful orientation and sampling
Cytology: cells from smear, fluid or fine needle aspirate, for screening or rapid diagnosis
Cytology limitation: no architecture, invasion difficult to assess
Appropriate use based on clinical question
questions.explanation: The three specimen types answer different questions. Marking should reward matching specimen type to clinical purpose.
